abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Engineered T cells equipped with a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) have shown tremendous clinical success, but tumor-mediated stimulation of T cell inhibitory receptors leads to exhaustion, hampering durable remission in patients. Mitigation of this effect via checkpoint inhibition or genome editing to knockout the genes encoding for these receptors has shown promise. Yet, the side effects of these procedures require better alternatives. Targeted epigenome editing offers a potent strategy to alter gene expression without DNA modifications. Its hit-and-run mechanism enables durable, multiplexed modulation of gene expression with greater safety. Here, we describe multiplexed epigenome editing inactivation of two critical-exhaustion-related genes, PDCD1 and LAG3, both in primary human T cells and in prostate-cancer-specific CAR T cells. Epigenetically modified CAR T cells are indistinguishable from parental cells across a range of functional assays. Although the model does not fully mimic T cell exhaustion, limiting functional assessment, gene silencing remains durable across multiple divisions and repeated CAR stimulations. Furthermore, transcriptomic analysis revealed minimal off-target effects not directly attributable to the effectors used. We demonstrate that targeted epigenome editing is effective and safe for multiplexed gene inhibition and holds potential in engineering CAR T cells with enhanced and customizable features.

sec.p: Keywords: MT: Delivery Strategies, epigenome editing, immunotherapy, CAR T cells, immune checkpoints, prostate cancer, PD-1, LAG-3

abstract.p: Epigenome editing is used to engineer CAR T cells targeting prostate cancer by stably silencing the PDCD1 and LAG3 genes, which encode key inhibitory checkpoint receptors. This DNA break-free approach enhances safety by avoiding genomic damage and holds promise as a next-generation strategy for safer, more durable cancer immunotherapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cancer immunotherapies exploit different strategies to instruct the patient’s own immune system to recognize and eliminate cancer cells that escaped immune surveillance. These include the use of biological molecules, such as cytokines or antibodies, which facilitate the mounting of an immune response against the cancer cells, the use of vaccines to induce immunological memory against tumor antigens, or the exploitation of viruses capable of preferentially infecting and replicating in transformed cells and inducing oncolysis.1 More recently, the use of adoptively transferred T cells engineered to recognize a specific tumor antigen via selected T cell receptors or chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) has revolutionized the field of immunotherapy with unprecedented success.2 However, the increasing number of patients infused with such cellular immunotherapies has also highlighted that complete remission cannot always be achieved.3 This has been attributed to the continuous exposure of the effector cells to the cancer antigen that inhibits the development of a memory T cell phenotype. Eventually this situation progresses to an “exhaustion” state characterized by reduced proliferation and upregulation of multiple checkpoint inhibitors. These are in turn stimulated by their respective ligands expressed by the tumor cells or by other cells in the tumor microenvironment to inhibit intracellular pathways involved in T cell function.4 Interruption of this negative loop has become an attractive strategy to overcome T cell exhaustion, and strategies combining adoptive T cell therapy with immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) have shown remarkable success as evidenced inter alia by the award of the Nobel Prize to the developers of this concept in 2018.5 Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) or programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockers in particular have shown impressive results in the clinic.6 Interestingly, further studies have demonstrated that combined blockade of multiple immune checkpoints produces synergistic effects.7,8 Given the non-trivial side effects of the systemic administration of ICB,9,10 genome editing strategies have been exploited to inactivate the genes encoding for these receptors with the goal of restoring T cell function.11,12 The favorable outcome achieved both in preclinical and clinical settings is encouraging but given the complexity of T cell physiology, altering these intrinsic pathways generally requires multiplexed editing strategies that may be associated with substantial genotoxic risks.13,14,15 Alternative editing strategies that allow multiplexed manipulation without DNA alterations are therefore desirable. Targeted epigenome editing involves the addition or removal of epigenetic marks at a specific locus with the goal of inducing stable and durable changes in gene expression without altering the underlying genomic sequence.16 Epigenome editors are proteins or protein complexes composed of a DNA-binding module that provides specific targeting capabilities, linked to one or more effector domains necessary to rewrite the epigenetic mark at the target site, resulting in either gene reactivation or gene silencing. We have previously described designer epigenome modifiers (DEMs) consisting of a TALE-based DNA-binding domain and two types of effector domains: (1) the Krüppel-associated box (KRAB) and (2) a fusion between the catalytic domain of the human de novo DNA methyltransferase 3A (DNMT3A) and the C-terminal domain of the murine regulatory factor Dnmt3L to further enhance enzymatic activity. This particular structure is capable of inducing DNA methylation and histone 3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) at endogenous target loci, leading to heterochromatin formation and sustained gene silencing in primary T cells.17 In addition, we confirmed the high specificity of DEMs through an extensive study of potential off-target effects.18 Here, we sought to exploit the DEM technology to mitigate CAR T cell exhaustion by multiplexed inactivation of two model checkpoint inhibitory receptors. We engineered DEMs targeting the promoter regions of either PDCD1 or LAG3 genes and demonstrated efficient and sustained multiplexed gene silencing that resisted repeated T cell activation or CAR-mediated chronic stimulation. Analysis of off-target effects proved specificity of the DEMs and promote the use of epigenome editing as an effective and safe strategy for multiplexed alteration of complex cellular pathways.

sec.title: DEMs mediate sustained multiplexed epigenome editing in primary T cells
sec.p: To identify an epigenome editor capable of effectively silencing the PDCD1 gene, we generated six DEMs engineered to target cis-regulatory regions of the PDCD1 gene (P1#1 to P1#6).19 In particular, four DEMs targeted the cis-regulatory region B (CRB) and two DEMs targeted the cis-regulatory region C (CRC), located 100 bp and 1.1 kb upstream of the transcription start site (TSS), respectively (Figure S1A). These DEMs were previously assessed for their ability to induce silencing of a reporter gene in a dedicated cell line,19 and we further tested them here in primary human T cells allowing the selection of P1#5 as the most effective for PDCD1 gene silencing (Figure S1B). Similarly, to silence the expression of the LAG3 gene, we engineered two DEMs (L3#1 and L3#2) to bind its proximal promoter, in a region located between 10 and 150 bp upstream of the TSS (Figure S2A). When tested in primary human T cells, both LAG3-specific DEMs induced up to 1.8-fold reduction in LAG3 expression (Figure S2B), and we selected L3#1 for further experiments. For simultaneous PDCD1 and LAG3 silencing, we transiently delivered in vitro transcribed (IVT) mRNA encoding either P1#5 or L3#1 via electroporation into primary human T cells activated 3 days earlier following a protocol well established in our laboratory.20 All cells belonging to the different electroporation groups recovered well within a few days showing viability and proliferation ability comparable to those of control cells (Figure S3). To ensure long-term assessment of the silencing, the transfected cells were kept in culture for a total of 39 days by reactivating them regularly on days 7, 17, 27, and 37 to trigger the expression of PD-1 and LAG-3 receptors and enable their detection 2 days after (Figure 1A). Flow cytometry analysis performed on day 19 post-transfection showed a 2.7- and 2.3-fold decrease in the frequency of PD-1+ cells in the samples receiving either P1#5 alone or in combination with L3#1, respectively, as compared to the sample receiving an unrelated DEM. Similarly, we measured a 1.8- and 2.1-fold decrease in LAG-3+ cells in the sample transfected either with L3#1 alone or in combination with P1#5, respectively (Figures 1B and S4A). The decrease in PD-1+ and LAG-3+ cells was persistent throughout the duration of the experiment and up to 39 days post-transfection, thus enduring to four cycles of T cell activation and demonstrating the stability of the epigenome editing at each target locus (Figures 1C and S5). To confirm that the reduced surface level of the two receptors is consequent to reduced gene transcription as an effect of epigenome editing, we measured PDCD1 and LAG3 transcript levels at day 19 post-transfection. Accordingly, PDCD1 transcript levels were 3.8- and 2.2-fold lower in samples receiving either P1#5 or P1#5 in combination with L3#1, respectively, as compared to control. Similarly, LAG3 transcript levels were 1.8-fold lower in both test samples (Figure 1D). These results suggest that gene silencing occurs at the transcriptional level. Since the DEMs exert their repressive activity through the deposition of de novo DNA methylation,17 we measured the DNA methylation levels via bisulfite sequencing on day 19 post-transfection, in a genomic region centered on the respective DEM targets. This comprised 19 and 10 CpG sites for PDCD1 and LAG3, respectively. In both regions, total DNA methylation levels were highly increased, reaching up to 4.9- and 3.6-fold higher values in samples receiving both DEMs at PDCD1 or LAG3 loci, respectively, compared to controls (Figures 1E and 1F). Although we limited our bisulfite sequencing to the immediate surrounding of the DEM-binding sites, our previous work suggest that the methylation mediated by a DEM can be spread up to ±2 kilobases from the binding site.17 As expected, in line with the sustained downregulation of PD-1 and LAG-3 protein levels through day 39, we observed a strong inverse correlation between CpG methylation and surface expression across all conditions, supporting the persistence of DEM-induced promoter methylation over time (Figure S6). Notably, methylation levels were similar in samples receiving the single DEM or both, underlying that multiplexed epigenome editing occurs independently at the target loci and is not compromised by the simultaneous presence of multiple epigenome modifiers. Importantly, when observing the DNA methylation pattern across the different CpG sites included in the analysis, it was found to peak in proximity of the DEM-binding sites at both loci with CpGs #12 and #13 being the most methylated in PDCD1 gene and CpGs #3, #4, and #5 in LAG3, respectively. Again, methylation pattern followed a similar distribution in samples receiving the single DEM or both (Figure 1G).

sec.title: Transcriptomic analysis confirms the safety of multiplexed epigenome editing in primary T cells
sec.p: DNA targeting technologies, such as the DEM used in this study, may suffer from unspecific interaction of the DNA-binding domain with unwanted genomic region, thus altering off-target gene expression. To dissect the specificity profile of the P1#5 and L3#1 DEMs used herein, we analyzed the transcriptome of T cells that underwent epigenome editing via bulk-RNA sequencing on day 19 post-electroporation. We analyzed cells isolated from three different healthy donors that went through the same procedure and isolated RNA 2 days after the second activation to ensure the T cells would be in a metabolic state typically associated with PDCD1 and LAG3 genes activation (Figures 1A and S7). Principal-component analysis (PCA) revealed that inter-donor variation represented the major source of difference between the different samples analyzed that clustered by donor identity (Figure S8). To identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) resulting from DEM off-target activity and exclude changes induced by the procedure, we compared cells receiving the P1#5 and L3#1 DEMs to control cells that were only pulse electroporated (mock control). This analysis revealed a total of 32 and 34 DEGs in the sample receiving either the P1#5 or the L3#1 DEM, respectively. In both cases, the target genes were among the highly significant downregulated genes with 3.4-fold decrease in PDCD1 expression and 1.8-fold decrease in LAG3 expression in the respective samples. Interestingly, simultaneous delivery of P1#5 and L3#1 DEMs resulted in increased alteration of gene expression with the identification of 338 DEGs. Again, PDCD1 and LAG3 were among the most significantly downregulated genes with 3.7- and 1.9-fold decrease in their expression levels, respectively (Figure 2A; Table S1). Gene ontology analysis performed using the complete set of DEGs indicated that both downregulated and upregulated genes were significantly enriched in diverse biological processes and cellular components related to chromatin remodeling, metabolism, and cell proliferation in line with the activated status of the cells (Figure S9).

sec.p: Despite the large number of DEGs identified, most of these genes were upregulated and many of them are significantly enriched in immune-related biological processes, including (1) T cell activation, (2) regulation of cytokine production, and (3) lymphocyte proliferation. These enrichments suggest that at least part of the observed transcriptional upregulation may be a biological consequence of PDCD1 and LAG3 silencing, rather than an unintended off-target effect. The removal of inhibitory signaling through the silencing of these immune checkpoints could plausibly result in a more activated transcriptional state, even in the absence of direct stimulation by checkpoint ligands. Additional mechanisms may also contribute, including (1) transient transcriptional responses to DEM mRNA electroporation, (2) indirect secondary effects from altered signaling dynamics, and (3) off-target effects independent of DNA-binding site specificity. We, therefore, excluded the upregulated genes as direct effect of DEM off-targeting (Table S1) and hypothesized that a direct DEM off-target site would lead to downregulated gene expression in both samples receiving the same DEM. Thus, we compared the significantly repressed genes identified in the samples receiving either the P1#5 or the L3#1 DEM alone with those in the samples receiving both DEMs. This comparison returned seven significantly downregulated genes in both groups receiving the P1#5 DEM and eight genes in the groups receiving the L3#1 DEM, respectively (Figure 2B). In addition, one downregulated gene appeared in both the single-DEM conditions and was therefore excluded as unlikely to represent a true sequence-specific off-target. We also identified three genes that were consistently downregulated across all DEM-treated samples. Since these changes occurred irrespective of the specific DEM used, we consider them unrelated to targeted binding activity and more likely reflective of general transcriptional responses to the delivery procedure (e.g., mRNA electroporation) or other non-specific cellular stress.

To verify that the consistently downregulated genes were a consequence of direct DEM off-target activity, we performed an in silico analysis using the online tool COSMID21 to identify potential off-target binding sites of the used DEM. Allowing up to three mismatches with each corresponding target site, we retrieved 3,439 and 2,218 potential binding sites within the human genome for the P1#5 and L3#1 DEMs, respectively (Table S2). A more detailed analysis showed that only one among these predicted off-target binding sites was in proximity of the THEMIS gene identified as significantly downregulated in both groups receiving the P1#5 DEM (Figure 2C). However, fine positioning of the potential binding site excluded a direct DEM silencing effect, as this site mapped to a site that was located 26,257 bp from the respective TSS (Table S2). To evaluate the impact of DEM activity on genes located in proximity of the respective DEM target sites, we examined the expression levels of all the genes within 1 Mb of the PDCD1 and LAG3 targets, respectively. Importantly, none of these genes were significantly downregulated (Figure S10).

sec.title: Multiplexed epigenome editing in a CAR T cell model is sustained upon antigen stimulation
sec.p: Once established the conditions to achieve precise, efficient, and sustained multiplexed epigenome editing in primary human T cells, we adapted the strategy to a CAR T cell model. We chose a second-generation CAR engineered with a CD28 co-stimulatory domain and a CD3ζ signaling domain targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), previously described by our team.22 To enable multiplexed epigenome editing in CAR T cells, we adjusted our culturing protocol to combine the transduction of a γ-retroviral vector encoding the CAR construct with the transfection of mRNAs encoding the DEM system, respectively (Figure 3A). Following editing, both epigenome-edited CAR T cells and corresponding controls were expanded for 2 weeks before functional assessment. Remarkably, epigenome-edited CAR T cells demonstrated robust recovery following the editing procedure, reaching expansion levels comparable to mock-electroporated control cells by the end of the culture period, despite both groups experiencing a substantial initial cell loss due to the electroporation step itself (Figure S11A). In contrast, CAR T cells subjected to multiplex genome editing via CRISPR-Cas9 for simultaneous inactivation of PDCD1 and LAG3 exhibited high levels of inactivating mutations (Figure S11B) but showed slower recovery during expansion. By the end of the 2-week culture period, their cell numbers were significantly lower compared to controls (Figure S11A). This disparity is likely attributable to DNA damage responses activated by genome editing, which involves DNA double-strand breaks, an effect absent in epigenome editing approaches23 (Figure S11B).

sec.p: After the expansion, we first confirmed that transduction efficiency was not compromised by the epigenome editing step with the population of CAR+ cells following a similar trend as in non-transfected control cells (Figure S12). We then measured the efficiency of epigenome editing in reducing the surface expression of PD-1 and LAG-3. To this end, cells were co-cultured with antigen-positive cells (i.e., the PSMA+ cell line C4-2) for 48 h in order to induce CAR-mediated activation, which in turn results in PDCD1 and LAG3 overexpression. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that all the test samples were effectively activated, with over 80% of the T cells showing acquisition of the CD25 marker, a commonly used indicator of T cell activation (Figures 3B and S13). Importantly, as a consequence of effective epigenome editing, cells transfected with DEM-encoding mRNA showed reduced surface expression of PD-1 and LAG-3 as compared to non-transfected control, according to the DEM combination received. Importantly, we measured 2.8- and 2.3-fold reduction in the fraction of PD-1+ cells as compared to non-transfected control, in single and in multiplexed editing, respectively. Similarly, we achieved 1.5-fold reduction in LAG-3+ cells in both conditions tested (Figures 3C and S4B). To confirm that the reduction of PD-1+ and LAG-3+ cells was stable, we sought to establish an assay in which the CAR T cells are repeatedly stimulated with antigen-positive cells. This persistent and long-term stimulation, also referred to as chronic stimulation, has been previously reported to result in progressive loss of T cell effector function and failure in tumor cell killing in CD19-positive tumor models.24,25 We therefore modified our protocol and replenished the culture with PSMA-positive cells (C4-2 cells) every 3 days for a period of 12 days (Figure 3A). At the endpoint, flow cytometry analysis confirmed the persistence of the PD-1 and LAG-3 reduction, which ranged between 2.4- and 1.7-fold for PD-1 and 1.8- and 2.9-fold for LAG-3, in single and in multiplexed editing, respectively (Figure 3D). Importantly, the reduction in surface expression correlated with a significant reduction in the corresponding PDCD1 and LAG3 transcript levels (Figure 3E) and likewise with a substantial increase in methylation levels at the DEM target sites (Figures 3F and 3G). Such results confirmed that again here we achieved similar silencing efficiency both in single and multiplexed editing condition.

sec.title: Multiplexed-epigenome-edited CAR T cells are fully functional and retain desirable anti-exhaustion features
sec.p: Having established the conditions for efficient and sustained multiplexed epigenome editing in CAR T cells, we considered of utmost importance to prove that these cells are equally powerful as non-modified CAR T cells. Although we lacked a system that recapitulates exhaustion in our chosen CAR T cell model, we performed a thorough in vitro assessment of critical parameters that define CAR T cell functionality driven by target antigen recognition. Importantly, testing our modified CAR T cells in the absence of PD-1 and LAG-3 canonical ligands, PD-L126 and MHC class II, respectively,27 allowed us to generate a proof of concept about the feasibility and safety of editing the epigenome in CAR T cells. Our in vitro assessment included cytotoxicity, secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and the ability to proliferate and develop a memory phenotype in response to target-specific stimulation. For this purpose, we co-cultured the PSMA-specific CAR T cells with a PSMA+ PD-L1− MHCII− target cell line (C4-2) (Figure S14). When co-cultured with increasing amounts of these target cells, the cytotoxicity profile of epigenetically edited CAR T cells was largely similar to that of non-transfected CAR T cells. At high tumor burden, exemplified by an effector to target (E:T) ratio of 1:32 and 1:16, epigenetically edited CAR T cells were significantly more efficient in tumor cell killing as compared to control CAR T cells (Figures 4A and S15). Importantly, non-transduced T cell controls did not elicit unspecific killing of the target cells (Figure 4A, dashed line). Similarly, culturing CAR T cells with the antigen-negative control cell line Du145 did not result in significant acute cytotoxicity, although slightly elevated background killing was observed compared to the antigen-positive cell line—consistent with previously published findings for this CAR T cell model (Figure S16).22 To further characterize the proper induction of T cell response against the tumor cells, we measured the levels of critical cytokines secreted in the culturing medium, such as interferon gamma (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), indicative of a pro-inflammatory response,28,29 and IL-2, related to T cell proliferation.30 In addition, we also quantified the release of the serine protease granzyme B, an important component of cytotoxic T cell granules.31 Our results show no significant differences between epigenetically edited and control cells in the secretion levels of any of the four analytes measured, with the major source of variability being the T cell donor’s source (Figure 4B). To assess whether epigenetically edited CAR T cells have a different ability to differentiate into effector T cells as compared to non-edited cells, we characterized the distribution of the different T cell subsets via flow cytometry. Unstimulated CAR T cells retained a central memory phenotype regardless of the epigenome editing step. Upon stimulation with antigen-positive C4-2 cells, all CAR T cells effectively acquired an effector phenotype again regardless of the epigenome editing step (Figure 4C). However, epigenetically edited CAR T cells showed reduced induction of PD-1 and LAG-3, with reduced number of cells expressing both checkpoint inhibitors at the endpoint (Figure 4D). Furthermore, epigenome editing did not significantly impact the ability of CAR T cells to proliferate upon repeated antigen encounters (Figure 4E). Remarkably, stronger reduction of surface PD-1 and LAG3 levels, achieved via multiplexed CRISPR-Cas9-mediated inactivation of the two corresponding genes, resulted in similar results (Figure S17). Indeed, both non-edited CAR T cells and those in which PDCD1 and LAG3 were inactivated using either genome or epigenome editing strategies exhibited similar behavior. Of note, the cytotoxicity assay under conditions of high tumor burden did not reproduce the differences observed previously when performed with T cells from a different donor, suggesting potential donor-dependent variability in the response (Figure S17D). Taken together, the thorough functional analysis described above did not reveal any adverse effects induced by the silencing of PDCD1 and LAG3 genes via multiplexed epigenome editing, suggesting that this proof-of-concept procedure is effective in producing CAR T cells with clinically recognized favorable properties.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The last decade has witnessed a major breakthrough in cancer immunotherapy. T cells equipped with specific CAR molecules have shown remarkable efficacy to recognize and eliminate tumor cells, in particular CD19-positive B cell lymphoma,32,33,34,35 acute lymphoblastic leukemia,36 and multiple myeloma.37,38 Nevertheless, a lack of favorable response to the CAR T cell therapy has been observed due to a variety of mechanisms including antigen escape, tumor microenvironment immunosuppression, limited CAR T cell persistence, and the appearance of exhaustion. For example, in B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, relapse rates after CD19 CAR T cell therapy are substantial. Of these, at least 20% of relapses involve antigen escape (CD19-negative disease), whereas other relapses are associated with CAR T cell dysfunction, including exhaustion.39 In multiple myeloma, recent studies of BCMA-targeted CAR T therapy have identified early relapse linked to transcriptional and functional profiles consistent with T cell exhaustion.40 These suggest that one of the leading causes of failure of this therapy dwells in the mechanism of T cell exhaustion.41,42 The trigger is still elusive but eventually leads to the establishment of a dysfunctional state of the T cells that acquire the expression of multiple checkpoint inhibitory receptors and progressively lose effector functions.43 As a result, CAR T cells are unable to respond to tumor cells as demonstrated in multiple clinical trials in which non-responders typically had increased levels of exhausted cells as compared to complete or partial responders.44,45 Recent evidence suggests that the tumor microenvironment is critical to elicit CAR T cell exhaustion. Besides the secretion of inhibitory molecules,46 the interaction between inhibitory ligands present on the tumor cell surface with the corresponding inhibitory receptors expressed by the CAR T cells is also crucial. These receptors normally act as breaks of the immune system, controlling the activity of immune cells to prevent damage to the host cells.47 However, tumor cells take advantage of this inhibitory pathway and upregulate the corresponding inhibitory ligands to engage the T cells and escape immunity. Blocking this interaction has provided encouraging results in clinical settings with significant increase in response rates and remission cases in different tumor groups.48 In addition, multiple preclinical studies have shown that CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockout of PDCD1 enhances CAR T cell cytotoxicity, persistence, and tumor control in murine xenograft models, particularly in PD-L1-expressing tumors.12 Similarly, LAG3 knockout has been shown to boost T cell function in vitro and in vivo,49 and dual disruption of PD-1 and LAG-3 can yield additive or synergistic effects in some preclinical systems.50 Importantly, these strategies are demonstrating improved response rates compared to canonical CAR T cells in a set of clinical trials, especially for PDCD1.51,52,53 However, the use of blocking antibodies, the induction of complete knockout, or silencing via short hairpin RNA (shRNA) of checkpoint genes may disrupt physiological regulatory mechanisms, potentially increasing the risk of T cell overactivation, terminal differentiation, or immune-related toxicity. Our epigenome editing approach avoids the adverse effects observed with systemic checkpoint blockade, the genotoxic risks derived from the use of DNA-cleaving enzymes used in genome editing approaches and RNAi-associated toxicity. Therefore, DEMs can be used to durably modulate target gene expression and enable simultaneous gene inactivation with greater safety. We have previously shown successful multiplex inhibition of two genes encoding the HIV entry co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4, using transient hit-and-run expression of specific DEMs in primary human lymphocytes.17 In this work, we leveraged our targeted epigenome editing system to generate CAR T cells lacking the expression of two critical checkpoint inhibitory receptors, namely PD-1 and LAG-3. PDCD1 gene expression is regulated by multiple mechanisms that involve two conserved cis-regulatory regions located 100 bp and 1.1 kb upstream of the TSS, named cis-regulatory region B (CRB) and cis-regulatory region C (CRC), respectively.54 To achieve robust PDCD1 gene silencing, we designed a total of six DEMs targeting these two regulatory elements and identified the most effective for successful gene silencing. Notably, as our targeted epigenome editing platform relies on simultaneous deposition of DNA methylation and histone-3 lysine-9 tri-methylation at the target site for gene silencing,17 the higher concentration of CpG sites in the CRC-C region might have contributed to better gene silencing efficacy when targeting this region. To silence LAG3 expression, we followed a similar strategy and designed two DEMs targeting the region of the LAG3 promoter with higher number of CpG sites. Importantly, the two effectors were similarly effective confirming the importance of altering DNA methylation to control gene expression when using DEMs. Having identified the best-performing epigenome editors, we established the conditions to achieve sustained multiplex gene silencing in primary T cells. As the stability of the deposited repressive mark is crucial for sustained silencing effect, we established a protocol for long-term in vitro culturing of the edited primary T cells over a period of almost 40 days. To this end, the cells were activated and induced to proliferate via T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation every 10 days. Besides the heavy proliferative stress that cells undergo during this culturing period, we show that the silencing of the two inhibitory receptors is maintained over time. This is a particularly important finding as both PDCD1 and LAG3 genes are upregulated during T cell activation. Thus, the persistence of silencing, combined with the strong negative correlation between promoter methylation and surface expression, suggests that the de novo epigenetic marks deposited by the DEMs are stably maintained reinforcing the durability of this editing strategy and resulting in a gene silencing effect that is dominant over physiological receptor upregulation. Having established the conditions to achieve effective and durable gene silencing that is resistant to TCR-mediated T cell activation, we thought to assess whether epigenome editing is effective in inducing gene silencing that resists CAR-mediated T cell activation. This is particularly critical in the clinical setting, as CAR T cells typically encounter tumor cells multiple times in a patient, resulting in continuous CAR-mediated T cell activation.55 We therefore established a protocol for multiplexed epigenome editing in CAR T cells by combining γ-retroviral transduction, to express a PSMA-specific CAR, and electroporation, to deliver in vitro transcribed mRNA coding for the selected DEMs. We demonstrate that epigenetically edited CAR T cells not only recovered effectively from the editing procedure, resulting in sustained reductions in PDCD1 and LAG3 expression, but also expanded more robustly than cells edited using mRNA-based CRISPR-Cas9 components. These findings underscore the advantages of employing a DNA-break-free strategy, which avoids the detrimental effects associated with genome editing, such as activation of DNA damage response pathways.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of a protocol to achieve effective multiplexed epigenome editing in CAR T cells. Based on our expertise in large-scale manufacturing of genome-edited CAR T cells,56 we anticipate this protocol can be easily adapted for efficient manufacturing of clinical-grade epigenetically edited CAR T cells. To demonstrate that the epigenome editing procedure does not impair CAR T cells activity, we performed a thorough in vitro functional characterization of the edited cells. Either single or multiplexed gene silencing did not affect the proliferative capacity of CAR T cells, cytokine secretion, and their ability to eliminate antigen-positive tumor cells. These results suggest that, from a functional point of view, epigenetically edited CAR T cells are largely indistinguishable from their non-edited counterparts. However, under conditions of high tumor burden, represented in vitro by a low effector-to-target ratio, epigenetically edited CAR T cells demonstrated enhanced tumor-killing activity (Figure 4A). However, when the assay was repeated using T cells from a different donor, this difference was not reproduced (Figure S17D). Although this variability likely reflects donor-specific differences, the initial result suggests a potential benefit that warrants further investigation in larger, more controlled studies and suggests a potential benefit from the reduced expression of inhibitory receptors even in the absence of their corresponding ligands on the cancer cell surface. Notably, functional assays revealed no significant differences between epigenetically edited cells and CRISPR-Cas9-edited cells, despite the latter achieving near-complete knockout of PDCD1 and LAG3. This finding suggests that the absence of functional benefits is not due to inefficient silencing achieved via epigenome editing, but rather reflects limitations of the in vitro assay system employed, which lacks the necessary ligands to trigger the PD-1 and LAG-3 inhibitory pathways. Future studies would benefit from incorporating these ligands, either by using patient-derived cells that naturally express them or by engineering the antigen-positive target cell line to display them on the surface.

Due to legitimate concerns about potential off-target effects, we assessed the impact of DEMs on the cellular transcriptome via RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). We hypothesized that off-target binding could impact chromatin structure and dysregulate the expression of genes. We retrieved significantly deregulated genes and excluded those genes that were upregulated considering that this effect could not be directly attributed to the binding of DEMs. We then considered as potential off-targets only those genes that were significantly downregulated in both samples receiving the same DEM. This analysis revealed a single potential off-target site of the P1#5 DEM in proximity of the THEMIS gene. While the distance of the potential off-target binding site from the TSS is too large to account for a direct effect on gene transcription, tridimensional chromatin structure might have resulted in proximity to the transcription start site, thereby inducing an alteration in gene expression. In alternative, the presence of a cryptic regulatory region might explain the impact on gene expression upon epigenome editing. Nevertheless, these findings suggest that epigenome editing off-target effects might be independent from the proximity of the binding site to the TSS and that the spatial distribution of chromatin within the nucleus might contribute to off-target effects. Although beyond the scope of this project, it will certainly be of interest in the future to further address the safety concerns of this technology. We can nonetheless conclude that DEM off-target effects are unlikely, in line with the principle that off-target epigenome editing outside of regulatory regions is generally silent. These results support further development of this technology to modulate gene expression, for example by strategically designing multiple DEMs to target distinct regulatory regions of a given gene, allowing for the evaluation of potential synergistic effects on repression strength.

Our work demonstrates that epigenome editing has an enormous potential to enhance CAR T cells by simultaneous and durable silencing, of key exhaustion-related genes, which resists stimulation and does not impair critical anti-tumor functions while providing desirable features that could be beneficial upon transplantation. Moreover, we propose that partial silencing, as achieved in our study, may preserve a level of physiological regulation and help balance safety with efficacy, helping mitigating the risks associated with total immune checkpoint abrogation, which has been linked to adverse effects in clinical checkpoint blockade therapies.57 The absence of genotoxic risks, the lack of overt off-target effects, and the scalability to large-scale manufacturing supports the exploitation of this technique for the generation of improved next-generation cancer immunotherapies.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This study aimed to develop a multiplexed epigenome editing approach to induce simultaneous and stable silencing of two key immune checkpoints in a manner that is compatible with the conventional generation of CAR T cells for clinical application. Given the dynamic nature of metabolic and epigenetic state in CAR T cells in response to target-mediated activation, a particular focus on the stability of the silencing was considered. To acknowledge the inter-donor variability inherent to the use of primary cells, at least three different donors were included in each experiment.

sec.title: DEMs design and cloning
sec.p: DEM target sites within the proximal promoters of PDCD1 and LAG3 genes (Figures S1A and S2A; Table S3) were identified fulfilling the following criteria: (1) the presence of a thymine as the first target base pair for optimal TALE binding; (2) proximity to annotated transcription-factor-binding motifs to secure chromatin accessibility and potentially compete with endogenous transcription activators58,59; and (3) minimal number of in silico predicted off-target binding sites.21 The TALE-based DNA-binding domains targeting the selected target sites were assembled as previously described60 and eventually cloned in the final DEM destination plasmid that includes the KRAB and a fusion between the catalytic domain of the human de novo DNA methyltransferase 3A (DNMT3A) and the C-terminal domain of the murine regulatory factor Dnmt3L.61 The DEM plasmids encoding the PDCD1 and LAG3 repressors have been deposited in Addgene and are available under the ID numbers #227738 (PDCD1-targeting DEM) and #227739 (LAG3-targeting DEM).

sec.title: In vitro mRNA transcription
sec.p: Expression plasmids containing the DEM coding sequence downstream of a T7 promoter were linearized using the PspOMI restriction enzyme and gel purified. One microgram of linearized plasmids was used in the in vitro transcription reaction, which was performed using the mMessage mMachine T7 Ultra Kit (Thermo Fisher, Massachusetts, USA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, the reaction was performed at 37°C for 2 h, followed by the poly(A) tailing reaction for 35 min at 37°C, to obtain capped and tailed mRNAs expressing the different DEMs. The resulting mRNA was recovered via lithium chloride precipitation according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Cell lines and primary T cell culturing conditions
sec.p: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from at least three different healthy donors were obtained from leukoreduction system (LRS) chambers by density gradient separation using Biocoll (Bio&SELL, Nuremberg, Germany). Primary T cells were obtained from PBMCs either by enrichment after activation or by negative selection using the EasySep Human T cell Isolation Kit (Stemcell technologies, Vancouver, Canada) to obtain a pure CD3+ cell population. The cells were cultured in RPMI complete medium, which includes RPMI 1640 GlutaMAX (Life technologies, Carlsbad, California), 10% FBS (PAN Biotech, Aidenbach, Germany), 1X penicillin-streptomycin, and 10 mM HEPES buffer (Sigma-Aldrich, San Luis, Missouri). Unless stated otherwise, this medium was supplemented with 100 U/mL rhIL-2 (ImmunoTools, Friesoythe, Germany). Medium was changed every 2–3 days depending on the rate of expansion. Prostate cancer cell lines C4-2 (PSMA+) and Du145 (PSMA−) were cultured in the same medium as T cells but without rhIL-2. All cells were maintained in culture at 37°C with 5% CO2.

sec.title: T cell manipulation
sec.p: Primary T cells (from PBMCs or isolated CD3+) were activated using an activation medium prepared by supplementing RPMI complete medium with ImmunoCult Human CD3/CD28/CD2 T cell activator (Stemcell technologies, Vancouver, Canada) at a final concentration of 10 μL/mL together with rhIL-2 at 100 U/mL. The same medium was applied for T cell reactivation. Activated T cells were electroporated on day 3 post-activation using the 4D nucleofector device (Lonza, Basel, Switzerland) with the P3 Primary cell kit S (Lonza, Basel, Switzerland) to deliver 8 or 16 μg of mRNA encoding for the DEMs P1#5 or/and L3#1 in 1 million cells using the pulse program EO-115, according to the manufacturers’ instructions. Immediately after the electroporation, cells were transferred to a well of a 96-well plate containing 180 μL fresh RPMI complete medium supplemented with rhIL-2 at 1,000 U/mL for optimal recovery. The rhIL-2 concentration was gradually reduced to 100 U/mL over the next 4 days. To monitor transfection efficiency, a control electroporation was routinely performed using 0.5 μg of PureBoost EGFP mRNA (Cellerna Bioscience, Germany), which consistently resulted in >90% GFP-positive cells.

In order to produce epigenetically edited CAR T cells, CD3+ cells were activated as described above and transduced 1 day later with a γ-retrovirus encoding for a previously published D7 scFv-based CAR designed to target PSMA.22 Briefly, 1 million cells suspended in the activation medium supplemented with rhIL-2 at 1,000 U/mL were plated in one well of a 48-well plate pre-treated with poly-D-lysine at 0.1 mg/mL (Sigma-Aldrich, San Luis, Missouri). Then, a volume of virus suspension sufficient to accommodate 300 TU/cell was incubated with protamine sulfate at a final concentration of 5 μg/mL for 5 min at room temperature before its addition to the cells to enhance transduction. The plate was then spinoculated at 1,600 RCF for 90 min to concentrate the virus on the surface of the plate. The transduced cells were left in culture for 2 days before electroporation as described above.

sec.title: Cell surface staining and flow cytometry
sec.p: Cell surface staining was performed using selected primary antibodies already coupled to defined fluorochromes to allow direct detection via flow cytometry. Between 50,000 and 100,000 cells were resuspended in the corresponding antibody mix according to manufacturer’s instructions. The following antibodies were used: anti-human CD25-PE (clone 4E3, Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany), anti-human CD25-APC (clone 4E3, Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany), anti-human CD279-FITC (clone NAT105, BioLegend, San Diego, California), anti-human CD223-PerCP-eFluor710 (clone 3DS223H, eBioscience, San Diego, California), anti-human CD62L-BV421 (clone DREG-56, BD Horizon, Franklin Lakes, New Jersey), anti-human CD45RA-FITC (clone HI100, BioLegend, San Diego, California), and the CAR F(ab')2 Anti-Human IgG-PE (Polyclonal, Southern biotech, Birmingham, Alabama).

sec.title: Quantification of transcript levels
sec.p: To quantify gene expression levels, a two-step RT-qPCR protocol was developed. In the first step, extracted RNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA using the QuantiTect Reverse Transcription Kit (Qiagen, Venlo, the Netherlands) following the manufacturers’ instructions. Having converted the RNA to cDNA, the Luna Universal qPCR Master Mix (NEB, Ipswich, Massachusetts) was employed to perform real-time qPCR following the manufacturers’ instructions for a 96-well plate format. To obtain relative expression levels, normalization against the reference gene beta-2-microglobulin (B2M) was chosen using the 2ˆ-ΔΔCt method.62 This was possible because the target and reference genes had similar amplification efficiencies. The primer sequences used can be found in Table S4.

sec.title: Quantification of DNA methylation levels
sec.p: Genomic DNA isolated from selected samples underwent bisulfite conversion using the EZ DNA Methylation-Gold Kit (Zymo research, Irvine, California), following the manufacturers’ instructions. The genomic sites of interest (Figures 1E and 1F) were amplified from the bisulfite-converted samples by PCR using the PyroMark PCR Kit (Qiagen, Venlo, the Netherlands). The primer sequences used can be found in Table S4. The amplicons were then cloned into pjet1.2 vector and analyzed by Sanger sequencing as previously described.61

sec.title: Assessment of CAR T cell functionality
sec.p: To detect the expression levels of the PSMA-specific CAR and allow normalization of cell density based on the amount of CAR+ cells prior to starting the functional assays, T cells were harvested on day 14 post-transduction and stained using a CAR-specific antibody (F(ab')2 Anti-Human IgG-PE, polyclonal, Southern biotech, Birmingham, Alabama) for detection via flow cytometry. Changes in T cell phenotype upon cancer cell encounter was assessed by co-culturing CAR T cells with C4-2 (PSMA+) cells for 48 h at an E:T ratio of 1:1 in RPMI complete medium without cytokines. After 24 h, cells were stained to detect the CAR, CD62L, and CD45 RA to identify the different T cell subsets. After gating on CAR+ cells, the classification was done by the following criteria: naïve and stem-cell like memory T cells (Tn, scm) are CD62L+ and CD45RA+, central memory T cells (Tcm) are CD62L+ and CD45RA−, effector T cells (Teff) are CD62L− and CD45RA+, and effector memory T cells (Tem) are CD62L− and CD45RA−. To assess the extent of T cell activation consequent to engaging of the cancer cells and to measure the extent of target gene silencing, the same co-culture was assessed 48 h later to detect the CAR, PD-1 (CD279), LAG-3 (CD223), and CD25 markers. In addition, at this time point, an aliquot of the supernatant was taken to evaluate the concentration of cytokines (TNF, IFN-γ, and interleukin-2 [IL-2]) and the protease granzyme B (Gr. B) by a multiplexed cytometric bead array (CBA) (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, New Jersey) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. To determine the cytotoxic effect of CAR T cells in killing antigen-positive tumor cells, we established a co-culture between PSMA-specific CAR T cells and either C4-2 (PSMA+) cells or Du145 (PSMA−) for 48 h at increasing E:T ratio. The viability of target cells (a measure of CAR T cells’ cytotoxicity) was assessed as a function of metabolic activity using the Proliferation Kit II (XTT) (Sigma-Aldrich, San Luis, Missouri). This colorimetric assay allows quantifying the viable cells based on their ability to cleave the XTT tetrazolium salt to produce a soluble formazan salt, whose absorbance is quantifiable according to manufacturers’ instructions. The inclusion of controls such as the culturing medium as well as single cultures of the CAR T cells or of the antigen-positive cell line allow for the calculation of CAR-mediated cytotoxicity. This is achieved by subtracting the background provided by the medium color as well as by the metabolic activity of the effector cells and using the culture with the antigen-positive cell line without CAR T cells as a reference. For the chronic CAR T cell stimulation assay (Figure 3A) CAR T cells were co-cultured with irradiated C4-2 cells at a 1:1 E:T ratio over the course of 12 days. Irradiation was performed using the Cesium source IBL637C (CIS Bio-International, Codolet, France) for a 30 Gray exposure one day prior co-culture. Every third day, CAR T cells were harvested and counted before their addition to newly irradiated C4-2 cells, keeping the 1:1 E:T ratio. The total number of CAR+ cells was used to determine population doubling (PD), which is obtained by calculating the log2 of the ratio between the numbers of cells harvested by the number of cells seeded. The cumulative PD, indicative of cell proliferation, was computed as the sum of all the values obtained. Cells collected at the endpoint of this assay were assessed for PD-1 and LAG-3 expression levels via both flow cytometry and RT-qPCR. In addition, bisulfite sequencing was performed to corroborate the durability of the DNA methylation marks deposited through the action of the DEMs.

sec.title: RNA sequencing and analysis
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from cell pellets harvested on day 19 post-electroporation, using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Venlo, the Netherlands) by following the manufacturers’ instructions. The Smart3-seq method was used to generate the sequencing library.63 Sequencing data were aligned to the reference genome using STAR v2.7.10b.64 Subsequently, bioinformatics analysis and visualization were performed in the R environment. EdgeR v4.0.2 was used to perform differential expression analysis using a design matrix that corrects for donor and batch information. Common and tagwise dispersion was estimated with the negative binomial generalized linear model (GLM) method (functions: estimateGLMCommonDisp and estimateGLMTagwiseDisp). The GLM method was then used to retrieve the differentially expressed genes (functions: glmFit and glmLRT). To predict potential off-target binding sites of the P1#5 and L3#1 TALE-based DNA-binding domains, we used COSMID21 allowing for up to three mismatches with the intended target site and without insertions or deletions. Predicted off-target sites were annotated with ChIPseeker.65 Data visualization was performed with various packages: VennDiagram v1.7.3 for the Venn Diagrams; PCA plots with pcaExplorer v.2.28.0; Volcano Plots with EnhancedVolcano v1.20.0; and heatmaps with pheatmap v1.0.12.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses indicated in the corresponding figure legends were performed with the assistance of GraphPad Prism 10.

sec.title: Data availability
sec.p: Next-generation sequencing datasets have been deposited in Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) accession number GSE273682. All other data generated or analyzed during this study are included in the Table S5. All the corresponding DEM-encoding plasmids are available from the authors upon request.
